newsitem.title: KENYA: Political tension seen threatening Kenyan economy.
newsitem.headline: Political tension seen threatening Kenyan economy.

text.p: The acid test for Kenya in the run-up to elections this year will be whether it reins in political tension and rekindles fast evaporating investor confidence, economic analysts said on Tuesday.
They were speaking a day after an outbreak of the worst political violence since pluralist politics were introduced in 1991.
Monday's political clashes, reminiscent of the torid election period in 1992, left up to 10 people dead and scores injured and hospitalised across Kenya.
Financial analysts feared that gains in Kenya's economy -- largely due to economic reforms -- could be wiped away by the volatile political climate.
Kenya has forecast economic growth at 4.0 percent in 1997 compared to 4.6 percent in 1996 and 4.8 perfcent in 1995. That compared to no growth in the 1991 to 1992 period.
Inflation is forecast in single digits compared to around 101 percent through most of 1992.
Kenya's opposition, usually divided on ethnic, ideological and personal lines, has found a fragile cohesion in its campaign for constitutional reforms before elections later this year.
The confrontation between the opposition and Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi seems likely to continue and the hardline standoff is getting investors running scared.
Market indicators showed swift response on Monday.
The Nairobi stock exchange index edged up 17.46 points but traded volume fell to the year's low at 5.1 billion shillings on 140,382 shares.
An executive at a multi-national corporation added: "This (violence) is a double blow. Firstly because the message we are getting is that instability is here to stay unless reforms are carried out.
"Secondly a stronger message to investors and business houses is that the government is losing control or is not even in control," he said.
Western donors, who underwrite lifeblood aid amounting to over $900 million a year to the region's economic and diplomatic engine, are also begining to rethink.

The United States ambassador, Prudence Bushnell, told a university forum on Monday that Kenya has not fulfilled its promise as a bright hope of democracy. The envoy said elements by which polls could be viewed as free and fair were not in place.
"The fact that Kenyans must witness once again pre-election confrontations indicates that persistent and serious problems still exist in the transition to full democracy," she said.

But economic experts said what was more worrying was that the political temperature was rising just as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was closing in on Moi's government because of concerns about its handling of a multi-million dollar financial scandal.
The IMF has delayed the release of a $36 million loan to Kenya.
The Fund has also given the government until the end of July to respond to its concerns or face the potential suspension of its Enhanced Structual Adjustment Facility loan agreement.
The delay in disbursement of the loan -- it had originally been slated for approval at the end of last month -- was a blow to Moi at a time of mounting protests inside Kenya against his rule.

"The political confrontation could not have come at a wrong time for Moi. IMF certification is very important, actually it is the lifeblood for any Third World country and what donors and the business is hearing from the IMF is not good news," said a senior government economist.

"Yesterday's (Monday) political fiasco is dreadful public relations for the country. It is bound to impact negatively on the economy. My business relies on law and order and I am concerned at what is happening," said a leading manufacturer.
But leading stock broker and investment manager John Munge cast a positive view.
"This is an election year and there is bound to be tension but I do not think it will get out hand," said Munge.
